objectives: Reason about food web + apex predator decline.
Connect coral reefs + fisheries to ecology.

slides.title: Vertical zones: euphotic, mesopelagic, bathypelagic, abyssal, hadal
slides.body:
The ocean is vertically stratified into ecological zones based on light + depth + community composition:

• **Euphotic (sunlit, 0-200 m)**: 1% surface PAR (photosynthetically active radiation) reaches ~200 m. All photosynthesis happens here. Phytoplankton, zooplankton, fish, marine mammals. ~95% of fisheries catch.
• **Mesopelagic (twilight, 200-1000 m)**: insufficient light for photosynthesis; some bioluminescence. Cold + dark. Massive biomass of small mesopelagic fish (myctophids, bristlemouths, lanternfish) — possibly the most numerous vertebrates on Earth. Daily vertical migration: zooplankton + fish rise at night to feed in surface, descend by day to escape predators. **Carbon-pump contributor**.
• **Bathypelagic (midnight, 1000-4000 m)**: total darkness. Pressure 100-400 atm. Cold (~2-4 °C). Sparse biomass; gigantism (giant squid, giant isopod). Specialized food acquisition (filter feeders, dead-fall scavengers).
• **Abyssal (4000-6000 m)**: ocean floor across most basins. Sediment habitats (mud, ooze, manganese nodules). Sea cucumbers, brittle stars, deep-sea fish.
• **Hadal (6000-11000 m)**: trenches (Mariana, Kermadec, Puerto Rico). Specialized fauna; only recently explored.

**Light + biology**: depth of euphotic zone varies from ~10 m (turbid coastal) to ~200 m (clear oligotrophic gyres). Compensation depth = where photosynthesis equals respiration (~1% surface light).

**Biomass distribution**: surface 200 m has ~75% of total ocean biomass; mesopelagic ~20%; deep sea ~5%. But by individual count, mesopelagic fish may outnumber all other vertebrates combined.

slides.title: Horizontal zones + biomes
slides.body:
Surface ocean divides into **biomes** based on temperature, productivity, light:

• **Tropical** (between Tropic of Cancer + Capricorn, ~30°N to 30°S): warm, oligotrophic gyres in the centers; productive marginal zones (Indonesian Throughflow, Caribbean). Coral reefs concentrated here.
• **Subtropical**: oligotrophic gyres; very low chlorophyll; characteristic clear blue water.
• **Temperate**: seasonal cycle of stratification → spring/fall blooms → productive fisheries (cod, herring, anchovy).
• **Polar**: ice-influenced; seasonal sea ice + ice algae; restricted light in winter, productive in summer.

**Coastal + neritic** zones (continental shelf, <200 m bottom):
- ~10% of ocean area but ~50% of fisheries productivity.
- Sub-tidal kelp forests, mangroves, sea-grass beds.
- Estuaries: where rivers meet ocean; nutrient-rich, juvenile-fish nurseries.

**Iconic ecosystems**:
- **Coral reefs** (warm tropical, 25-29 °C): biodiverse, dependent on symbiotic algae (zooxanthellae). Hosting ~25% of marine species despite <0.1% area. Bleaching + acidification under threat.
- **Mangroves**: tropical/subtropical coastal forests. Nurseries for fish + invertebrates; coastal protection; major carbon sequestration.
- **Kelp forests** (cold temperate): subtidal/intertidal seaweed canopies. Sea otters as keystone (trophic cascade: otters → urchins → kelp).
- **Salt marshes + seagrass beds**: shallow coastal vegetation; high productivity + carbon storage.
- **Hydrothermal vent communities**: chemosynthetic (not photosynthetic) — tube worms, vent mussels, vent shrimp. Sulfur + hydrogen chemistry. Discovered 1977 (Galapagos Rift); revolutionized biology by showing life independent of solar energy.
- **Cold-water coral reefs**: along continental shelves at 100-1000 m. Slow-growing, fragile, threatened by bottom trawling + acidification.
- **Polar systems**: under-ice algae communities, krill-dependent food webs (krill → whales/penguins/seals). Vulnerable to ice loss.

slides.title: Food webs + apex predator decline
slides.body:
Marine food webs are organized by **trophic levels**:

• Primary producers (phytoplankton, kelp, seagrass): convert sunlight to organic matter. ~50 GtC/yr global.
• Primary consumers (zooplankton, herbivorous fish): eat producers.
• Secondary consumers (small predatory fish, krill-eaters): eat herbivores.
• Apex predators (sharks, tuna, marine mammals, sea birds, large fish): top of food web.

**Trophic transfer efficiency**: ~10% per level. So 10 kg phytoplankton → 1 kg zooplankton → 0.1 kg herbivorous fish → 0.01 kg predator. Apex predators have small populations because of the trophic pyramid.

**Industrial fishing impact** (FAO + Pauly):
- Global catch peaked around 1996 (~100 million t/yr); now ~80-90 Mt/yr; *unreported* catch may add 20-30%.
- Top predator biomass declined ~90% from pre-industrial (Myers + Worm 2003). Large tuna, marlin, swordfish populations decimated.
- 'Fishing down the food web' (Pauly+ 1998): mean trophic level of catch dropping over time → catch shifts to smaller species as larger ones depleted.
- Bycatch + discards: ~40% of catch wasted; trawling damages seafloor habitats.
- Illegal, unreported, unregulated (IUU) fishing: ~20% of global catch.

**Conservation responses**:
- Marine Protected Areas (MPAs): ~8% of ocean designated; ~3% fully protected. UN 30x30 target (30% by 2030).
- Quota systems (TAC — Total Allowable Catch), individual transferable quotas (ITQs).
- Fisheries certifications (MSC — Marine Stewardship Council).
- International agreements (UNFSA — UN Fish Stocks Agreement; CCAMLR — Antarctic; BBNJ — Beyond National Jurisdiction 2023 treaty).
- Aquaculture: now > capture fisheries by tonnage (~110 Mt/yr); growing fast; environmental concerns (waste, antibiotics, escapees, feed sourcing).

Long-term picture: marine biodiversity has declined ~50% since 1970s. Climate change + acidification + warming + overfishing compounding. Restoration depends on rapid + coordinated action — 30x30 + carbon mitigation key.

question.question: Apply trophic-level math to a fishery
question.goal: An apex predator (5th trophic level, e.g., tuna) requires how much primary production per kg of biomass?

steps.prompt: If transfer efficiency is 10% per trophic level + the predator is at trophic level 5 (primary producer = level 1), what's the multiplier?
steps.reveal: Trophic level 5 needs 1/0.1⁴ = 10,000× phytoplankton biomass. Equivalent to 10,000 kg phytoplankton → 1 kg predator.

steps.prompt: If 1 kg of tuna has the same biomass per area as 0.0001 kg phytoplankton, what does that imply for ocean fisheries?
hints: Apex predators must be rare because of the pyramid.
steps.reveal: Apex predators *must* be rare; even modest harvesting can deplete their standing stock far more easily than primary producers (which are essentially inexhaustible from harvesting). Tuna populations have crashed under industrial fishing because the trophic pyramid limits sustainable yield.

steps.prompt: What's the maximum sustainable yield (MSY) concept's implication?
steps.reveal: MSY = catch rate that maximizes long-term yield, given logistic population dynamics. Theoretically achieved at ~50% of carrying capacity (K). For tuna: catching > MSY causes population decline; catching < MSY underuses the resource. In practice, MSY is hard to estimate (uncertainty in K, growth rate, recruitment) → fisheries scientists use precautionary approaches with adaptive management.

hints: Apex predators easiest to find + most valuable.
steps.reveal: Pauly+ 1998 'fishing down marine food webs': large predators (tuna, marlin, swordfish, large cod) most valuable + easiest to catch → depleted first. Catch shifts to smaller, lower-trophic species (sardines, anchovies, even krill). Mean trophic level of global catch has dropped ~0.1 per decade. Ecological + economic consequence: total catch can't keep up; some populations may not recover; ecosystem function altered.

question.question: Order these ocean zones by *typical biomass density* (highest to lowest).
question.explanation:
Biomass density gradient (approximate):
• **Kelp forest / coral reef**: highest density per unit area — multi-tier biomass + photosynthetic productivity comparable to tropical rainforest.
• **Upwelling region surface**: nutrient-replete + light-rich; supports massive primary + secondary production (Peruvian, Benguela, California upwelling regions).
• **Continental shelf / temperate**: highly productive; seasonal blooms; major fisheries.
• **Open ocean surface (subtropical gyre)**: oligotrophic; low chlorophyll. Vast area but low density.
• **Mesopelagic**: still has substantial biomass (mesopelagic fish thought to be most numerous vertebrates on Earth) but low concentration per m³.
• **Abyssal seafloor**: lowest biomass density; sparse + slow-metabolism communities.

Total ecosystem productivity reflects biomass × area; coastal + shelf ecosystems have small area but high density, accounting for ~50% of global fisheries. Open-ocean gyres are individually low-productivity but huge area, accounting for ~30% of marine NPP. Mesopelagic + deep + abyssal: emerging research recognizes their large total contribution to carbon cycling + biodiversity.

question.question: Why do coral reefs host such extraordinary biodiversity (~25% of marine species in <0.1% area) despite oligotrophic surface waters?
options: Symbiosis with zooxanthellae (photosynthetic dinoflagellates in coral tissue) provides energy + carbon — coral hosts get ~90% of energy from zooxanthellae photosynthesis, recycling N + P in tight loops. Reefs build vertically + horizontally, creating 3D structural complexity → many habitat niches. Trophic complexity supports diverse predator-prey + symbiosis networks. Tropical light + temperature provide stable productivity. The combination of structure + symbiosis + stable environment fosters speciation + coexistence.
Coral reefs are in nutrient-rich water.
question.explanation:
**Why coral reefs are biodiverse**:

1. **Coral-algal symbiosis (zooxanthellae)**: Symbiodinium dinoflagellates live in coral tissue at densities ~10⁶/cm². Photosynthesize using sunlight + coral-respired CO₂ + N waste. Translocate ~90% of fixed C to coral host as glucose, glycerol, amino acids. In exchange, coral provides protected habitat + nitrogen/phosphorus access. **Tight nutrient recycling** lets reefs flourish in low-nutrient tropical surface water.

2. **Structural complexity**: corals build CaCO₃ skeletons; over 100s-1000s of years, reef structures grow vertically + horizontally → 3D habitat matrix. Each crevice + cave + overhang is a microhabitat → many niches.

3. **Trophic complexity**: ~4,000+ fish species + ~600 coral species + tens of thousands of invertebrate species. Predator-prey, mutualism, cleaner-host, parasite-host relationships → high biotic interaction.

4. **Stable tropical environment**: T 25-29 °C year-round, high light, low seasonality — favoring specialization.

5. **Long evolutionary history**: tropical reef-building corals have been present in some form for ~250 million years; many lineages diversified in tropical reef habitats.

**Reef threats**:
- **Bleaching** (warming): zooxanthellae expelled when T exceeds ~30-32 °C; coral starves; if persistent, dies. 1998, 2010, 2014-17, 2024 mass bleachings.
- **Ocean acidification**: reduces aragonite saturation; impairs calcification.
- **Crown-of-thorns + diseases**: outbreaks killed large reef areas.
- **Overfishing + pollution**: ecosystem cascades + algal overgrowth.
- **Storms**: typhoons + cyclones can devastate but reefs historically recovered.

**Status**: ~50% of global reef cover lost since 1950s. Great Barrier Reef (Australia): 5 mass bleachings 2016-2024. Caribbean: ~80% cover lost. Indo-Pacific somewhat better but degrading.

**Restoration**:
- Selective breeding of heat-tolerant corals
- Coral nurseries + outplanting
- Marine Protected Areas
- Watershed management (reduce runoff, sewage, nutrients)
- Emissions reduction (long-term solution)

Reefs are an early-warning case for ocean health: visibly declining; biodiversity + ecosystem services lost; sentinel for climate impact.

hints: What enables high diversity in oligotrophic water?
slides.workedSolution: Coral-zooxanthellae symbiosis: dinoflagellates photosynthesize using sunlight; provide ~90% of coral energy via translocated organic matter; tight N + P recycling lets reefs thrive in low-nutrient tropical surface water. Structural complexity from CaCO₃ skeletons creates 3D habitat matrix → many niches. Trophic + symbiotic + parasitic relationships → ~25% of marine species in <0.1% area. Threats: bleaching (warming expels zooxanthellae), acidification, disease, overfishing. ~50% of global reef cover lost since 1950s. Restoration + emission reduction key.

question.question: If primary production in a region is 200 g C/m²/yr + transfer efficiency is 10% per trophic level, what's the maximum biomass of trophic-level-4 fish (e.g., cod) in g C/m²/yr?

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain why Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) — even small ones — have outsized effects on fisheries + ecosystems.
question.rubric: Mentions: MPAs prohibit / restrict fishing within boundaries. Inside MPAs: fish populations recover; large + old fish accumulate. Old + large fish have orders-of-magnitude higher fecundity (e.g., a 60-cm cod produces 100-1000× more eggs than a 30-cm cod). Spillover: adult fish migrate out + larval fish drift out → seed surrounding fishery. Result: MPAs increase regional fisheries productivity, not just local biodiversity. Examples: Cabo Pulmo (Mexico), Great Barrier Reef no-take zones, California Channel Islands. Required: ~20-30% of habitat in MPAs to be ecologically meaningful (UN 30x30 target). MPAs work best in combination with watershed management + fisheries reform + climate action. Concludes: MPAs are not just biodiversity reserves but functional fisheries-management tools; design + enforcement matter. Compliance + adaptive monitoring critical for success.
